original.target_description: Unassigned side: placeholder only; not examined.

replication.target_description: Replication Study 1 of original Study 2: scrambled-sentence analytic versus control priming, BCTI conspiracy beliefs; primary full-sample between-condition post-test comparison, p. 4 §4.2. Sample located in p. 3 §4.1.1.3.

n.sample_role: Participants completing both waves and passing quality checks, in primary between-condition BCTI analysis (147 experimental, 155 control).
n.exclusions: 316 completed both waves; 14 removed for failing preregistered quality checks in either wave. Exclusion criteria in §4.1.1.2 include time limit, Prolific approval, attention and bot/fraud checks; no speeders. Separate robustness analyses exclude one outlier or 16 hypothesis guessers and are not the primary test.
n.quote: A total of 316 UK Prolific participants completed both ... one of the two waves (n = 14), we ... were left with N = 302 participants (147 in the experimental and 155 in ... the control condition).

reported_success.quote: Overall, we found no evidence that the analytical prime group ... decreased in belief in conspiracy theories. On the contrary, we found ... evidence for the null hypothesis, i.e., that the scrambled sentence ... analytical priming manipulation did not influence belief in conspiracy ... theories.

notes: Identity independently checked within the supplied canonical text: UvA repository cover and article title identify No evidence that priming analytic thinking reduces belief in conspiracy theories; authors Većkalov, Gligorić and Petrović; DOI 10.1016/j.jesp.2023.104549; JESP 110 (2024), 104549.
